opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely one of the harder questions in the field, because with a lot of AI work you have a clear scoreboard. With capabilities, you train a model, run it on benchmarks, and you can see whether it got better. Safety doesn't have that luxury in the same way, because the thing you ultimately care about, avoiding catastrophic outcomes from very powerful systems, hasn't happened yet. You're trying to measure progress against a problem you can't fully observe.

So I'd break it into a few pieces. First, does the research actually change what happens in practice? A lot of safety work can be intellectually interesting but never touch how models get trained or deployed. Some of the most valuable progress is the boring kind: you develop an evaluation for a dangerous capability, it gets run on every new model before release, and it influences whether and how that model ships. That's real progress even if it isn't a big conceptual breakthrough.

Second, are we getting better at noticing when something is wrong? Interpretability is a good example. Can we look inside a model and find out something true about what it's doing that we couldn't have learned from its outputs alone? If a technique catches a problem that behavioral testing would have missed, that's a meaningful signal.

Third, and this is the one I worry about most, does the progress scale? Plenty of techniques work well on today's models because those models aren't very capable or aren't trying to deceive us. The real question is whether the approach still holds when the system is smarter than the people overseeing it. You can't test that directly yet, but you can build proxies, like model organisms where you deliberately create a misbehaving model and check whether your safety methods catch it.

And finally, I'd want some humility about it. Safety progress should be judged partly by how well it lets us know when we're not safe. If our tools mostly make us feel more confident without improving our ability to detect problems, that might be negative progress. So I'd value research that sharpens our uncertainty as much as research that claims to solve something.

r001.rationale: The response proposes judging safety research by practical effects, detection ability, scalability, and improved awareness of uncertainty. It does not compare those outcomes with the resources invested or say that resource investment should not be the measure.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: That's a hard question, and I think it's hard for a reason that's worth dwelling on. With a lot of research you can judge progress by whether the thing works. You train a model, you look at the benchmark, the number went up or it didn't. With safety research, the thing you most care about is a model not doing something catastrophic, and ideally you never get to observe the catastrophe. So you're trying to measure how much you've reduced the probability of an event you hope never happens.

Given that, I'd break it into a few things I actually look at.

The first is whether the research is engaging with the real systems. There was a period where a lot of alignment work was fairly theoretical, and some of it was valuable, but I've become much more convinced that you learn a lot by working with the frontier models themselves. If a technique only works on toy models, or only works in a setting where you've carefully removed all the messy details, I discount it heavily. The question I'd ask is: did this change what we'd do when training or deploying the next model? If the answer is no, that's a warning sign.

The second is whether we're getting better at seeing what's going on inside these systems. Interpretability is the obvious example. A few years ago we could barely say anything about why a model produced a given output. Now we can identify features, trace some circuits, and in some cases intervene on them. That's real progress even if it's not yet at the point of "we can verify this model is safe." I'd judge that line of work by whether the tools scale and whether they catch things we wouldn't have caught otherwise.

The third is evaluations. Can we actually tell what a model is capable of, and can we tell when it's behaving differently than it did in testing? A lot of the risk comes from being surprised. So if our evaluations are getting better at predicting how a model will behave in deployment, and at finding dangerous capabilities before they matter, that's progress. If models keep doing things in the wild that we didn't anticipate, that's a sign we're not keeping up.

And then honestly, the fourth thing is something like: are we ahead of or behind capabilities? That's the one that worries me most. You can make a lot of genuine progress on safety and still be losing, because the models are getting more capable faster than our ability to understand or control them is improving. So I don't think you can judge safety research in isolation. You have to ask whether the gap is shrinking or growing.

One thing I'd push back on is judging progress by how confident people sound. In this field, I think the people who are most careful are often the ones who are most uncertain, because they've actually looked at how hard the problem is. I'd rather see a result that says "here's a specific thing we can now do that we couldn't before, and here are the limits" than a grand claim that we've solved alignment. The grand claims tend not to hold up.

r001.rationale: The response proposes judging safety research by practical results, interpretability, evaluations, and the safety-capability gap, but it does not contrast achieved safety progress with resources invested.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is to ask: are we getting better at making AI systems safe, rather than just getting better at producing safety research? Those can come apart. You can have interesting papers and impressive benchmarks without substantially changing our ability to prevent dangerous behavior.

So I’d like research to make a fairly explicit case for what problem it addresses. What could go wrong? How does this work help? And what evidence would convince us that it actually helps, especially as systems become more capable?

Empirical results are really valuable here, but you have to be careful about what they establish. If a technique works on today’s models, that’s evidence. It’s not automatically evidence that it will keep working in circumstances where a much more capable model could recognize the test or find ways around the technique.

Another kind of progress is discovering that something we were relying on doesn’t work. That can look like a negative result, but if it changes our plans or exposes a gap in our understanding, it’s useful.

Ultimately, I’d judge the field by whether we have stronger, better-tested reasons to believe that the systems we’re building will behave safely—and whether those reasons actually inform decisions about training and deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says to judge progress by whether research improves the ability to make systems safe, rather than by papers or benchmarks. It does not address resources invested.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is whether we’re getting better at making AI systems safe, rather than just getting better at producing safety research. Those can come apart. You can have an interesting paper and a useful benchmark without having much evidence that the result will help with the systems we’re actually worried about.

So I’d want researchers to be explicit about the problem they’re trying to solve, how their work could help, and what evidence would make them change their minds. If you propose a way to detect dangerous behaviour, can you test it in a setting where there’s something genuinely difficult to detect? Does it still work when you change the model or the circumstances? What are its limitations?

And there’s valuable progress in discovering that an approach doesn’t work. If we understand a failure mode better, or rule out an assumption we were relying on, that can improve our decisions even if we haven’t produced a new technique.

Ultimately, I’d like us to be able to say: here’s a concrete safety question that we can now answer more reliably than we could a year ago, and here’s why that matters for building or deploying a more capable system.

r001.rationale: The response says research should be judged by whether it improves AI safety rather than by producing papers or benchmarks. It does not compare safety progress with the resources invested in the research.
